title: Our honest wellness journey (we did it wrong)
summary: A Season 3 bonus episode answering listener questions about body image, diet and working out. Cherie and Jean share their own history with weight gain, calorie counting, juice cleanses and unhealthy Peloton goals, and land on a philosophy of sustainable routines, one health pillar at a time, forgiving yourself, and being 'strong, not skinny'.

ideas.idea: Your relationship with your body is made of three elements: genetics (uncontrollable), upbringing (mostly uncontrollable but can be mitigated), and your everyday routine (controllable).
ideas.detail: The sisters grew up with a single mom, lots of microwave dinners and Hot Pockets, no desserts except orange juice and fruit, rice rather than bread, and no pressure about weight, which shaped what they crave today.

ideas.idea: Weight gain usually comes from unnoticed shifts in eating patterns when your environment changes, such as starting college or a new job.
ideas.detail: Jean gained weight in college eating a full panini for lunch, a big sushi roll for dinner, Egg McMuffins and unlimited desserts; Cherie gained 15-20 pounds in junior year of high school from daily salami sandwiches during the inactive winter months and lost it by switching to filling salads with tuna or vegetables.

ideas.idea: A lot of women have disordered eating that passes as normal because diet culture is so popularized; counting every calorie and weighing yourself daily is not actually normal.
ideas.detail: Jean's first restrictive phase, calorie counting and daily weigh-ins, started after her college weight gain; she later did three-day juice cleanses with coworkers every few months and once packed six bottles of juice into her ski bag for a Beaver Creek trip, which she now calls dumb.

ideas.idea: Diet alone will not make you healthy: two years of eating only Just Salad at Goldman while working 90-100 hour weeks and sleeping four to five hours still led to weight gain.
ideas.detail: Goldman's 200 West building was designed so you never leave (cafeteria, doctor's office, gym with laundered gray t-shirts and shorts, competitive heart-rate spin classes), but a 45-minute workout does not compensate for a desk-bound body, terrible sleep and weekend binge drinking.

ideas.idea: Health rests on four pillars, diet, exercise, sleep and stress/cortisol, and if all are bad at once you should pick one to work on rather than tackling everything.
ideas.detail: There is no silver bullet; at different points in life all, none or one of the pillars are working. Set an intention on one pillar at a time and accept that the routine for each area does not have to stay the same for your whole life.

ideas.idea: Crazed fitness kicks are not sustainable and are how burnout happens; the goal is a routine that fits your life today and is repeatable.
ideas.detail: Jean's Goldman associate Alexander Cochran tried SoulCycle two-a-days across the street from the office in 2010 and lasted a week. Jean's sustainable version came at Zynga, where she ran a few miles every morning before showering and eating breakfast at her desk.

ideas.idea: If you are in a grueling season where you truly could not do better, do not be hard on yourself: 'I'm doing the best I can every day' is a sufficient mantra.
ideas.detail: Looking back at two years at Goldman, Jean concludes she was just trying to survive and could not have done better; Cherie uses a Spotify meditation several times a week that opens with that mantra.

ideas.idea: Gamify consistency with a stretch challenge you can feel good about even if you miss it, like trying to go to the gym 30 days in a row and celebrating a 10-day personal record.
ideas.detail: Cherie has never hit 30 but is the most consistent she has ever been; Jean argues for baking in flexibility (e.g. five rest days within 30) so the goal is actually reachable. The test is whether the goal still lets you feel successful when you fall short.

ideas.idea: Metrics-driven fitness goals can become unhealthy: Cherie's pandemic rule of beating a Peloton personal record every ride made her skip workouts on days she did not feel 100%.
ideas.detail: She now recognizes she can be extreme and unforgiving with herself, so the 30-day challenge is explicitly framed as not a punishment.

ideas.idea: Stop outsourcing how you feel to the scale; judge your body qualitatively and intuitively, and accept a winter weight and a summer weight.
ideas.detail: Jean stopped weighing herself after her scale's batteries died a year ago and never replaced them; her daily mood used to depend on the number. Activity and daylight differ by season, so a single year-round goal weight does not make sense.

ideas.idea: Buy clothes you love in two sizes, and stop fixating on being a size 26 when you look and feel better in a 27 or 28 at different times of the year or your cycle.
ideas.detail: One of Jean's best friends buys Reformation dresses in two sizes; the hosts say if you have the expendable income you should do this for everything you love.

ideas.idea: Pick workouts suited to your body and your current phase of life rather than what is trendy; HIIT and Barry's are not for everyone.
ideas.detail: Jean felt nauseous and lightheaded in HIIT classes and quit Barry's (loud music, 25-30 people, no individual attention, injury risk); both used to run 3-6 miles a day and half marathons but no longer run. Finding what works takes experimentation and can change over time.

ideas.idea: Do the hardest thing first: if getting to the gym is the hardest part of your day, go first thing in the morning, because a 5 PM plan will be put off.
ideas.detail: Cherie admits she loves how she feels after working out but not the activity itself, and is drawn to lying in bed scrolling. Jean instead relies on an 'appointment mechanic', booking a class with a no-show strike so she cannot skip.

ideas.idea: Sign up for a race (5K, 12K or half marathon) as a forcing function to train consistently, ideally with friends who hold you accountable.
ideas.detail: Jean used half marathons to scare herself into working out until it stopped working and she winged one race day without training, which she does not recommend without a plan.

ideas.idea: Where you live and who your friends are largely determine your health: New York social life is brunch and drinks, while San Francisco and LA are daytime cities where hiking or biking with friends is normal.
ideas.detail: Wherever you live, deliberately find people who want activity as the form of hanging out, e.g. pickleball or new-grad sports leagues; Cherie joined a dodgeball league for the social element and is going on a pickleball date, and both are drinking much less.

ideas.idea: Feed your gut microbiome by targeting 40 different fruits, vegetables, legumes and nuts a week, as a stretch goal you do not punish yourself for missing.
ideas.detail: Cherie picked this up from a gut-health documentary on a Delta flight; the thesis is that the gut controls sleep and attention. With Cherie cooking, the sisters hit 40 for a couple of weeks and dropped to about 30 in weeks without grocery shopping.

ideas.idea: Set goals so you can reach 100%: Jean's annual '36 things to do at 36' list has 70 items so hitting 36 counts as full success.
ideas.detail: This contrasts with Cherie's stretch-goal mindset; both agree the point is being intentional rather than punishing yourself.

ideas.idea: Systems, guardrails and frameworks (like the 40-plant target or morning gym time) matter because the sisters know they will default to processed food and inactivity without them.
ideas.detail: They are candid that part of the motivation is vanity and looking good at a certain weight, but the mantra has shifted to 'strong, not skinny', which Cherie has written on her wall with 'skinny' crossed out.

ideas.idea: Changes never happen overnight; you are the captain of your own ship, and results come from consistency over weeks and months.
ideas.detail: Cherie says she has never had an extreme relationship with food because she always understood progress is on a delayed timeline; if she feels bad about her body, the answer is to go to the gym more consistently, not to purge or starve.
